domains.name: Domain D2: bias due to deviations from the intended interventions (the effect of assignment to the interventions)

questions.details:
Look in: the methods on blinding and on what each group received (its look, taste, route and schedule), and the results on adverse effects.
Y: the trial was open-label, or the interventions could not be disguised, for example surgery against a drug, or a talking therapy against a waiting list.
PY: the paper says participants were blinded, but something would likely have given the group away to many of them, such as an effect felt only on the active treatment or a dosing schedule that differed between groups.
PN: the paper says participants were blinded and reports nothing that would have broken it, but gives little detail.
N: a matching dummy made the groups impossible to tell apart, and nothing reported would have given the group away.
NI: the paper does not say whether participants knew.
questions.headline: Did the participants know which intervention they were getting while the trial ran?

questions.details:
Look in: the methods on blinding of clinicians, nurses, therapists or anyone else giving care, and on whether the interventions or their effects looked different.
Y: the trial was open-label for staff, or the staff had to give interventions that differ visibly.
PY: staff blinding is claimed, but something likely showed them the group, for example a treatment that shifts routine test results in a way staff would notice, or staff who also enrolled participants and could see the allocation.
PN: staff are said to be blinded and nothing reported would have broken it, but the paper gives little detail.
N: staff could not tell the interventions apart and nothing reported would have shown them a participant's group.
NI: the paper does not say whether staff knew.
questions.headline: Did the staff treating the participants or delivering the interventions know each participant's group while the trial ran?

questions.details:
Applies only when: the participants or the staff knew the group, probably knew it, or the paper does not say whether they did. If both participants and staff were, or probably were, unaware, answer NA.
Look in: the results and discussion for crossover, added treatments or extra attention, and for why they happened.
Y: the paper reports departures driven by knowing the group, for example staff giving one group extra care or tests, or participants adding treatments on their own because they knew their group.

NI: the paper does not report whether anyone received something other than their group's intervention.

questions.details:
Applies only when: departures from a group's planned intervention happened, or probably happened, because of being in the trial and not as routine care would have it. If there were none, probably none, or the paper does not say, answer NA.
Look in: how many participants were affected in each group, and whether the extra or different care acts on this outcome.
Y: the departures were frequent or large, and act on this outcome, so the result would plausibly differ without them.
PY: an effect on this outcome is likely, though not certain.
PN: an effect on this outcome is unlikely, though it cannot be excluded.
N: the departures could not plausibly reach this outcome, for example because the extra care does nothing for it.
NI: the paper does not describe the departures well enough to judge.
questions.headline: Could those trial-driven departures have changed the result for this outcome?

questions.details:
Applies only when: such departures happened, or probably happened, and they changed, probably changed, or may have changed the result for this outcome (the paper leaving that open counts). Otherwise answer NA.
Look in: the counts of each kind of departure, group by group.
Y: each kind of departure happened about as often in every group.
PY: the counts reported point to an even spread without showing it fully.
PN: the counts reported point to more, or different, departures in one group.
N: one group clearly had more of them, or a different kind.
NI: the paper does not give the departures group by group.
questions.headline: Were those trial-driven departures spread evenly across the groups?

questions.details:
Look in: the statistical methods for the analysis population (intention-to-treat, full analysis set, per-protocol and so on), and the flow diagram for who was analysed in each group.

Second: was anyone left out for a reason other than having no result for this outcome? Leaving out people found after randomisation never to have been eligible is acceptable when that finding could not depend on their group.
Y: both checks pass, as in an intention-to-treat analysis.
PY: the paper's description points to such an analysis but does not state it fully.
PN: the paper's description points to an analysis by treatment received, or one limited to participants who followed the protocol, without stating it fully.
N: either check fails, for example participants were counted under the treatment they actually got, or only those who completed their assigned intervention were analysed.
NI: the paper does not say who was analysed for this outcome, or under which group.

questions.details:
Applies only when: this outcome was not, or probably was not, analysed with everyone in their randomised group, or the paper does not say how it was analysed. If it was, or probably was, answer NA.
Look in: the flow diagram and the results tables, for how many were left out or moved in each group. Set that beside the number of events, or beside the size of the difference between the groups.
Ask: if those participants were put back in their randomised groups, could the difference between the groups change materially? Even a few can matter: when those participants were sicker or healthier than the rest, or when there are so few events that each one counts.
Y: yes, the change could be material.
PY: the numbers suggest a material change is likely.
PN: the numbers suggest any change would be small.
N: so few were affected that the result could not change materially.
NI: the paper does not report how many were left out or moved.

domains.name: Domain D3: bias due to missing outcome data

questions.details:
Look in: the flow diagram and the results tables, for the number randomised in each group and the number whose result for this outcome is in the analysis. Y: no result is missing, or only a handful by this test.
PY: the numbers given suggest only a handful are missing, without showing it exactly.
PN: the numbers given suggest more than a handful are missing.
N: more than a handful are missing.
NI: the paper does not say how many participants have a result for this outcome.

Applies only when: more than a handful of randomised participants have, or probably have, no result for this outcome, or the paper does not say how many. If results are, or probably are, complete or missing for only a handful, answer NA.

PY: such checks are reported, but only in part, for example the paper says the result held without showing the numbers.
PN: the checks give little comfort, for example one alternative analysis resting on a single guess.
N: the paper reports no such checks. An analysis that puts a value into each gap and then treats the data as complete shows nothing about whether the gaps distort the result.
NI: not allowed for this question. If the paper is silent, answer N.

Y: the reasons given are, or could well be, tied to how participants were doing, for example they stopped coming because they got worse, got better, or had a side effect.

questions.details:

PY: the signs lean that way, without being clear.
PN: the signs lean the other way.
N: none of these signs is present; or the authors show that, once participants' starting characteristics are taken into account, who went missing tells nothing more about the outcome.
NI: the paper gives too little to look for these signs.
questions.headline: Is there a concrete sign, beyond mere possibility, that whether results went missing depended on what they would have been?

domains.name: Domain D4: bias in measurement of the outcome

questions.details:

Y: the method fails at its job: it is known to give misleading readings for this outcome, or most participants already sit at the edge of its range, so a real change could not show.
PY: the description suggests a poor fit, without being clear.
PN: the method looks reasonable, though the paper says little about it.
N: the method is an accepted or validated way to measure this outcome.
NI: the paper does not say how this outcome was measured.
questions.headline: Was this outcome measured with a method that is unfit for it?

questions.details:
Look in: the methods and the schedule of visits. Ask whether anything about how the outcome was recorded differed by group: the tool or rule used to record it, or how closely each group was watched.
Y: something about how the outcome was recorded differed by group, for example one group had monthly scans and the other only a final one.
PY: the description suggests such a difference without stating it.
PN: the description suggests the same approach in every group without stating it.
N: nothing about how the outcome was recorded differed by group.
NI: the paper does not say how or when this outcome was assessed in each group.

questions.details:
Applies only when: the method of measuring this outcome was fit for it and the same in every group, or the paper does not say. If the method was, or probably was, unfit, or the outcome was, or probably was, measured differently between the groups, answer NA.

PY: the description suggests they knew, without stating it.
PN: the description suggests they were unaware, without full detail.
N: they were kept unaware of each participant's intervention.
NI: the paper does not say whether they knew.

questions.details:
Applies only when: whoever produced the values knew the intervention, probably knew it, or the paper does not say. If they were, or probably were, unaware, answer NA.
Look at: how the value comes about. Ask whether a person has to decide or interpret something for the value to exist.
Y: someone has to decide or interpret: the care team choosing to act (for example to operate, or to start a rescue treatment), a clinician grading severity or reading an image, or a participant rating how they feel.
PY: there is some room for interpretation.
PN: there is very little room for interpretation.
N: no one has to interpret anything, for example a laboratory value produced by an automated analyser.
NI: the paper does not describe the outcome well enough to judge.
questions.headline: Could knowing the intervention have swayed the value recorded for this outcome?

questions.details:
Applies only when: whoever produced the values knew, probably knew, or may have known the intervention (the paper not saying counts), and the values rest on judgement that this knowledge could, probably could, or might sway. Otherwise answer NA.
Look for: anything giving those people a stake in, or firm expectations about, the result, for example authors who devised the treatment doing the assessing, or participants recruited with the message that the new treatment works.
Y: such a stake or expectation is clear.
PY: it is likely but not documented.
PN: it is possible but nothing points to it.
N: there is no particular reason to expect the assessment was swayed.
NI: the paper gives too little to judge.

questions.details:
Look in: the trial registration, the protocol or statistical analysis plan the paper cites, and the dates it gives for them. Compare their outcome measure and analysis with the ones reported. A paper that only calls an outcome or analysis "prespecified", or cites a plan without saying what it fixes for this outcome, gives you nothing to compare.

PY: the paper describes what the plan fixes for this outcome (its measure and analysis) closely enough to compare, and the report follows it, but only the paper's word places the plan before the data by group were seen: it cites no registration, protocol or analysis plan for it, or cites one without a date that does.
PN: the report seems to depart from the plan, or there are signs that the plan was changed after the data by group could be seen.
N: the report departs from the plan without a reason unrelated to the results, or the plan was written or changed after the outcome data were seen.
NI: the paper names no plan settled in advance; or it names one but gives too little of what the plan fixes for this outcome to compare, even when it calls the outcome or analysis "prespecified"; or the plan's only date places it after the data by group were seen, such as a registration made late.

questions.details:

A measurement of a different outcome does not count. Only a plan written down before anyone could see the outcome data split by group (a registration, protocol or analysis plan) shows which versions were intended: a paper that reports a single version is not, by itself, evidence that only one was taken.
Look in: the outcome list and the date of the registration, protocol or analysis plan the paper cites, then the methods and the results. Which of the planned measurements have their results given in full?
Y: you can point to a measurement that the plan or the methods name whose result is missing or only summarised, while the one given in full is the more favourable, and the paper does not explain the choice. A primary outcome swapped for the registered one counts here.
PY: some measurements named in the plan or the methods have no results, but it is not clear the results guided which were shown.
PN: a plan fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the scale, its definition, the time point) and the report matches it, but only the paper's word places the plan before the data by group were seen: the paper cites no registration, protocol or analysis plan for it, or cites one without a date that does. A plan dated after the data by group were seen, such as a registration made late, is no such plan: answer NI. A plan that leaves any of these open, where the open part could have given a different result, is NI, not N or PN.
N: the paper cites such a plan (a registration, protocol or analysis plan whose date places it before the data by group were seen) that fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the scale, its definition, the time point), and the results include every version it names, or the authors give a reason unrelated to the results for any that is missing; or this outcome can be measured in only one way, for example death from any cause at the trial's single follow-up, so there was nothing to choose from.
NI: there is no such plan to hold the report against, or the plan leaves open something this result could have been chosen on, and this outcome leaves room for more than one version. Answer NI, not N, even when the paper itself shows only one version.

Look in: the analysis the plan describes and the plan's date, the analyses the methods mention, and the ones the results show. Note any analysis mentioned but not shown, and any result labelled post hoc.
Y: you can point to an analysis that was planned or mentioned whose result is missing or played down, while the one given prominence is the more favourable, and the paper does not explain the choice.
PY: the reported analysis differs from the planned one with no reason given, but it is not clear the results guided the choice.
PN: a plan fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the model, the covariates, the handling of missing results) and the reported analysis matches it, but only the paper's word places the plan before the data by group were seen: the paper cites no registration, protocol or analysis plan for it, or cites one without a date that does. A plan dated after the data by group were seen, such as a registration made late, is no such plan: answer NI. A plan that leaves any of these open, where the open part could have given a different result, is NI, not N or PN.
N: the paper cites such a plan (a registration, protocol or statistical analysis plan whose date places it before the data by group were seen) that fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the model, the covariates, the handling of missing results), and the reported analysis is that one, or the authors give a reason unrelated to the results for any difference; or this measurement can be analysed in only one way, so there was nothing to choose from. NI: there is no such plan to hold the report against, or the plan leaves open something this result could have been chosen on, and this measurement leaves room for more than one analysis. Answer NI, not N, even when the paper itself shows only one analysis.

Only the measuring is in question here, so an outcome you think poorly chosen can still be answered N.
Look in: the methods for the instrument, test, scale or definition and any reference to its validation, and the results for scores bunched at the top or bottom of the scale.
Y: the method fails at its job: it is known to give misleading readings for this outcome, or most participants already sit at the edge of its range, so a real change could not show.
PY: the description suggests a poor fit, without being clear.
PN: the method looks reasonable, though the paper says little about it.
N: the method is an accepted or validated way to measure this outcome.
NI: the paper does not say how this outcome was measured.
questions.headline: Was this outcome measured with a method that is unfit for it?

questions.details:
Look in: the methods and the schedule of visits. Ask whether anything about how the outcome was recorded differed by group: the tool or rule used to record it, or how closely each group was watched.
Y: something about how the outcome was recorded differed by group, for example one group had monthly scans and the other only a final one.
PY: the description suggests such a difference without stating it.
PN: the description suggests the same approach in every group without stating it.
N: nothing about how the outcome was recorded differed by group.
NI: the paper does not say how or when this outcome was assessed in each group.
questions.headline: Could this outcome have been measured, or its events found, differently in one group than in another?

questions.details:
Applies only when: the method of measuring this outcome was fit for it and the same in every group, or the paper does not say. If the method was, or probably was, unfit, or the outcome was, or probably was, measured differently between the groups, answer NA.
Who counts: the person whose report or judgement creates the value. For a questionnaire or diary that participants fill in, that is the participant; for a scan, a slide or an examination, it is the person reading or examining.
Y: they knew, for example participants in an open-label trial filling in their own questionnaire, or an unblinded investigator doing the examination.
PY: the description suggests they knew, without stating it.
PN: the description suggests they were unaware, without full detail.
N: they were kept unaware of each participant's intervention.
NI: the paper does not say whether they knew.
questions.headline: Did whoever produced this outcome's values know which intervention each participant had received?

questions.details:
Applies only when: whoever produced the values knew the intervention, probably knew it, or the paper does not say. If they were, or probably were, unaware, answer NA.
Look at: how the value comes about. Ask whether a person has to decide or interpret something for the value to exist.
Y: someone has to decide or interpret: the care team choosing to act (for example to operate, or to start a rescue treatment), a clinician grading severity or reading an image, or a participant rating how they feel.
PY: there is some room for interpretation.
PN: there is very little room for interpretation.
N: no one has to interpret anything, for example a laboratory value produced by an automated analyser.
NI: the paper does not describe the outcome well enough to judge.
questions.headline: Could knowing the intervention have swayed the value recorded for this outcome?

questions.details:
Applies only when: whoever produced the values knew, probably knew, or may have known the intervention (the paper not saying counts), and the values rest on judgement that this knowledge could, probably could, or might sway. Otherwise answer NA.
Look for: anything giving those people a stake in, or firm expectations about, the result, for example authors who devised the treatment doing the assessing, or participants recruited with the message that the new treatment works.
Y: such a stake or expectation is clear.
PY: it is likely but not documented.
PN: it is possible but nothing points to it.
N: there is no particular reason to expect the assessment was swayed.
NI: the paper gives too little to judge.
questions.headline: Is there a concrete reason, beyond mere possibility, to think that knowing the intervention did sway this outcome's values?

domains.name: Domain D5: bias in selection of the reported result

questions.details:
Look in: the trial registration, the protocol or statistical analysis plan the paper cites, and the dates it gives for them. Compare their outcome measure and analysis with the ones reported. A paper that only calls an outcome or analysis "prespecified", or cites a plan without saying what it fixes for this outcome, gives you nothing to compare.
Y: the paper cites such a plan, with a date that places it before the data by group were seen, and the plan fixes this outcome's measure and analysis; the report follows it, and any change was made before the data were seen or for a stated reason that has nothing to do with the results.
PY: the paper describes what the plan fixes for this outcome (its measure and analysis) closely enough to compare, and the report follows it, but only the paper's word places the plan before the data by group were seen: it cites no registration, protocol or analysis plan for it, or cites one without a date that does.
PN: the report seems to depart from the plan, or there are signs that the plan was changed after the data by group could be seen.
N: the report departs from the plan without a reason unrelated to the results, or the plan was written or changed after the outcome data were seen.
NI: the paper names no plan settled in advance; or it names one but gives too little of what the plan fixes for this outcome to compare, even when it calls the outcome or analysis "prespecified"; or the plan's only date places it after the data by group were seen, such as a registration made late.
questions.headline: Did this result come from an analysis that was planned, and written down, before anyone could see the outcome data split by group?

questions.details:
What counts as several measurements: more than one version of this outcome's result could have been reported, for example the same symptom rated on two questionnaires, or one score read at 6 and at 12 months. A measurement of a different outcome does not count. Only a plan written down before anyone could see the outcome data split by group (a registration, protocol or analysis plan) shows which versions were intended: a paper that reports a single version is not, by itself, evidence that only one was taken.
Look in: the outcome list and the date of the registration, protocol or analysis plan the paper cites, then the methods and the results. Which of the planned measurements have their results given in full?
Y: you can point to a measurement that the plan or the methods name whose result is missing or only summarised, while the one given in full is the more favourable, and the paper does not explain the choice. A primary outcome swapped for the registered one counts here.
PY: some measurements named in the plan or the methods have no results, but it is not clear the results guided which were shown.
PN: a plan fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the scale, its definition, the time point) and the report matches it, but only the paper's word places the plan before the data by group were seen: the paper cites no registration, protocol or analysis plan for it, or cites one without a date that does. A plan dated after the data by group were seen, such as a registration made late, is no such plan: answer NI. A plan that leaves any of these open, where the open part could have given a different result, is NI, not N or PN.
N: the paper cites such a plan (a registration, protocol or analysis plan whose date places it before the data by group were seen) that fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the scale, its definition, the time point), and the results include every version it names, or the authors give a reason unrelated to the results for any that is missing; or this outcome can be measured in only one way, for example death from any cause at the trial's single follow-up, so there was nothing to choose from.
NI: there is no such plan to hold the report against, or the plan leaves open something this result could have been chosen on, and this outcome leaves room for more than one version. Answer NI, not N, even when the paper itself shows only one version.
questions.headline: Was the result reported for this outcome chosen, because of what it showed, from among several measurements of it?

questions.details:
What counts as several analyses: the same measurement could have been analysed in more than one way, for example with and without outliers, or with two different statistical tests. Only a plan written down before anyone could see the outcome data split by group (a registration, protocol or statistical analysis plan) shows which analysis was intended: a paper that shows a single analysis is not, by itself, evidence that only one was run.
Look in: the analysis the plan describes and the plan's date, the analyses the methods mention, and the ones the results show. Note any analysis mentioned but not shown, and any result labelled post hoc.
Y: you can point to an analysis that was planned or mentioned whose result is missing or played down, while the one given prominence is the more favourable, and the paper does not explain the choice.
PY: the reported analysis differs from the planned one with no reason given, but it is not clear the results guided the choice.
PN: a plan fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the model, the covariates, the handling of missing results) and the reported analysis matches it, but only the paper's word places the plan before the data by group were seen: the paper cites no registration, protocol or analysis plan for it, or cites one without a date that does. A plan dated after the data by group were seen, such as a registration made late, is no such plan: answer NI. A plan that leaves any of these open, where the open part could have given a different result, is NI, not N or PN.
N: the paper cites such a plan (a registration, protocol or statistical analysis plan whose date places it before the data by group were seen) that fixes everything this result could have been chosen on (the model, the covariates, the handling of missing results), and the reported analysis is that one, or the authors give a reason unrelated to the results for any difference; or this measurement can be analysed in only one way, so there was nothing to choose from. That is rare: adjusting or not, the effect measure and the handling of missing results are each a choice.
NI: there is no such plan to hold the report against, or the plan leaves open something this result could have been chosen on, and this measurement leaves room for more than one analysis. Answer NI, not N, even when the paper itself shows only one analysis.
questions.headline: Was the result reported for this outcome chosen, because of what it showed, from among several analyses of the same measurement?

study.name: Domain D1: bias arising from the randomisation process (judged once for the trial)

questions.details:
Look in: the methods paragraph on randomisation, any supplement, and a protocol the paper cites.
Y: the paper names a chance mechanism, for example permuted blocks from statistical software or a randomisation website. Minimisation also counts as chance here.
PY: the paper names no mechanism, but what it does say makes a proper one the likely choice, for example the list was drawn up in advance by a statistician with no part in recruitment.
PN: details in the paper hint that the order could be foreseen, without saying so.
N: the group followed something other than chance that someone could know in advance and so predict or steer, for example the room a participant was admitted to.
NI: the paper says the trial was randomised and nothing about how.
questions.headline: Did chance alone decide which group each participant joined?

questions.details:
Look in: the methods, for who kept the allocation list, how the enrolling team learned each group, and whether enrolment came first.
Y: the group was released by a system or person outside the enrolling team, only once the participant was registered, so the team could neither foresee nor swap it.
PY: the paper names a safeguard of this kind but leaves gaps, for example it does not say who prepared the materials or when the group became known.
PN: the method the paper describes left the next assignment within the enrolling team's reach, for example materials kept by that team with no safeguard stated, though nothing shows anyone looked.
N: the enrolling team, or the participants, could see, predict or alter what came next, for example because the list was open to them or the order followed a pattern.
NI: the paper says nothing about how the assignment was kept from the enrolling team.
questions.headline: Was the next assignment out of reach of the people enrolling participants until each participant's enrolment was final?

questions.details:
Look in: the baseline table (characteristics by group) and the flow diagram's count randomised to each group; failing those, any sentence in the paper comparing the groups at the start. Judge from what is reported about the groups, not from the paper's account of how it randomised.
Y: something chance can hardly explain. In the baseline table: a strong predictor of this kind of outcome, or the outcome's own starting value, is unequal enough between groups to sway the result; many more rows differ than chance would give; or nearly every row matches too closely. In the flow diagram: group sizes far from the planned split.
PY: there are signs of this kind, but they are not clear-cut.
PN: nothing stands out, but the evidence is thin: the baseline table is short or leaves out characteristics that matter for this outcome, or the paper gives no numbers by group and only states in its text that the groups were alike at the start.
N: the baseline numbers for the randomised groups show them alike at the start, or differing only as much as random allocation would be expected to make them. One or two rows with a p-value under 0.05 in a long table are what chance alone produces.
NI: the paper says nothing about what the randomised groups were like at the start: no numbers by group and no statement comparing them. A table of only the participants who stayed to the end is not baseline numbers for the randomised groups.
questions.headline: Do the groups, as they stood at the start, look different in a way that hints the randomisation went wrong?

answers.question:
Did the participants know which intervention they were getting while the trial ran?
Look in: the methods on blinding and on what each group received (its look, taste, route and schedule), and the results on adverse effects.
Y: the trial was open-label, or the interventions could not be disguised, for example surgery against a drug, or a talking therapy against a waiting list.
PY: the paper says participants were blinded, but something would likely have given the group away to many of them, such as an effect felt only on the active treatment or a dosing schedule that differed between groups.
PN: the paper says participants were blinded and reports nothing that would have broken it, but gives little detail.
N: a matching dummy made the groups impossible to tell apart, and nothing reported would have given the group away.
NI: the paper does not say whether participants knew.

Did the staff treating the participants or delivering the interventions know each participant's group while the trial ran?
Look in: the methods on blinding of clinicians, nurses, therapists or anyone else giving care, and on whether the interventions or their effects looked different.
Y: the trial was open-label for staff, or the staff had to give interventions that differ visibly.
PY: staff blinding is claimed, but something likely showed them the group, for example a treatment that shifts routine test results in a way staff would notice, or staff who also enrolled participants and could see the allocation.
PN: staff are said to be blinded and nothing reported would have broken it, but the paper gives little detail.
N: staff could not tell the interventions apart and nothing reported would have shown them a participant's group.
NI: the paper does not say whether staff knew.

Did anyone depart from a group's planned intervention because of being in the trial, in a way routine care would not see?
Applies only when: the participants or the staff knew the group, probably knew it, or the paper does not say whether they did. If both participants and staff were, or probably were, unaware, answer NA.
Look in: the results and discussion for crossover, added treatments or extra attention, and for why they happened.
Y: the paper reports departures driven by knowing the group, for example staff giving one group extra care or tests, or participants adding treatments on their own because they knew their group.
PY: the paper does not say so outright, but what it reports makes such departures likely.
PN: the paper's account of the care given leaves little room for such departures, without ruling them out in so many words.
N: no departures happened; or the only ones are the sort routine care also sees, such as people stopping a treatment or skipping doses; or the protocol allowed them.
NI: the paper does not report whether anyone received something other than their group's intervention.

Could those trial-driven departures have changed the result for this outcome?
Applies only when: departures from a group's planned intervention happened, or probably happened, because of being in the trial and not as routine care would have it. If there were none, probably none, or the paper does not say, answer NA.
Look in: how many participants were affected in each group, and whether the extra or different care acts on this outcome.
Y: the departures were frequent or large, and act on this outcome, so the result would plausibly differ without them.
PY: an effect on this outcome is likely, though not certain.
PN: an effect on this outcome is unlikely, though it cannot be excluded.
N: the departures could not plausibly reach this outcome, for example because the extra care does nothing for it.
NI: the paper does not describe the departures well enough to judge.

Were those trial-driven departures spread evenly across the groups?
Applies only when: such departures happened, or probably happened, and they changed, probably changed, or may have changed the result for this outcome (the paper leaving that open counts). Otherwise answer NA.
Look in: the counts of each kind of departure, group by group.
Y: each kind of departure happened about as often in every group.
PY: the counts reported point to an even spread without showing it fully.
PN: the counts reported point to more, or different, departures in one group.
N: one group clearly had more of them, or a different kind.
NI: the paper does not give the departures group by group.

Does this outcome's analysis compare the groups as randomised, so that it estimates the effect of being assigned to an intervention?
Look in: the statistical methods for the analysis population (intention-to-treat, full analysis set, per-protocol and so on), and the flow diagram for who was analysed in each group.
Check two things. First: is everyone counted in the group they were randomised to, whatever they actually received? Second: was anyone left out for a reason other than having no result for this outcome? Leaving out people found after randomisation never to have been eligible is acceptable when that finding could not depend on their group.
Y: both checks pass, as in an intention-to-treat analysis.
PY: the paper's description points to such an analysis but does not state it fully.
PN: the paper's description points to an analysis by treatment received, or one limited to participants who followed the protocol, without stating it fully.
N: either check fails, for example participants were counted under the treatment they actually got, or only those who completed their assigned intervention were analysed.
NI: the paper does not say who was analysed for this outcome, or under which group.

domains.name: Domain D2: bias due to deviations from the intended interventions (the effect of assignment to the interventions)

answers.question:
For this outcome, is a result missing for none, or only a handful, of the randomised participants?
Look in: the flow diagram and the results tables, for the number randomised in each group and the number whose result for this outcome is in the analysis. A value the authors filled in themselves (imputed) counts as missing; so does a participant who withdrew before the end of follow-up in a time-to-event analysis.
To decide whether it is only a handful, picture the missing participants doing as badly as is believable in one group and as well as is believable in the other. If even that could not change what the result means, it is a handful. For a count of events, set the number missing beside the number of events: when the two are of similar size, it is not a handful.
Y: no result is missing, or only a handful by this test.
PY: the numbers given suggest only a handful are missing, without showing it exactly.
PN: the numbers given suggest more than a handful are missing.
N: more than a handful are missing.
NI: the paper does not say how many participants have a result for this outcome.

answers.question:
Did chance alone decide which group each participant joined?
Look in: the methods paragraph on randomisation, any supplement, and a protocol the paper cites.
Y: the paper names a chance mechanism, for example permuted blocks from statistical software or a randomisation website. Minimisation also counts as chance here.
PY: the paper names no mechanism, but what it does say makes a proper one the likely choice, for example the list was drawn up in advance by a statistician with no part in recruitment.
PN: details in the paper hint that the order could be foreseen, without saying so.
N: the group followed something other than chance that someone could know in advance and so predict or steer, for example the room a participant was admitted to.
NI: the paper says the trial was randomised and nothing about how.

Was the next assignment out of reach of the people enrolling participants until each participant's enrolment was final?
Look in: the methods, for who kept the allocation list, how the enrolling team learned each group, and whether enrolment came first.
Y: the group was released by a system or person outside the enrolling team, only once the participant was registered, so the team could neither foresee nor swap it.
PY: the paper names a safeguard of this kind but leaves gaps, for example it does not say who prepared the materials or when the group became known.
PN: the method the paper describes left the next assignment within the enrolling team's reach, for example materials kept by that team with no safeguard stated, though nothing shows anyone looked.
N: the enrolling team, or the participants, could see, predict or alter what came next, for example because the list was open to them or the order followed a pattern.
NI: the paper says nothing about how the assignment was kept from the enrolling team.

Do the groups, as they stood at the start, look different in a way that hints the randomisation went wrong?
Look in: the baseline table (characteristics by group) and the flow diagram's count randomised to each group; failing those, any sentence in the paper comparing the groups at the start. Judge from what is reported about the groups, not from the paper's account of how it randomised.
Y: something chance can hardly explain. In the baseline table: a strong predictor of this kind of outcome, or the outcome's own starting value, is unequal enough between groups to sway the result; many more rows differ than chance would give; or nearly every row matches too closely. In the flow diagram: group sizes far from the planned split.
PY: there are signs of this kind, but they are not clear-cut.
PN: nothing stands out, but the evidence is thin: the baseline table is short or leaves out characteristics that matter for this outcome, or the paper gives no numbers by group and only states in its text that the groups were alike at the start.
N: the baseline numbers for the randomised groups show them alike at the start, or differing only as much as random allocation would be expected to make them. One or two rows with a p-value under 0.05 in a long table are what chance alone produces.
NI: the paper says nothing about what the randomised groups were like at the start: no numbers by group and no statement comparing them. A table of only the participants who stayed to the end is not baseline numbers for the randomised groups.

N: more than a handful are missing.

questions.details:
Applies only when: more than a handful of randomised participants have, or probably have, no result for this outcome, or the paper does not say how many. If results are, or probably are, complete or missing for only a handful, answer NA.

Y: the authors re-ran the analysis under several believable guesses about how the missing participants fared, including guesses where those who left did worse or better than those who stayed, and the result held; or they used an analysis built to adjust for the missing results, not merely to fill the gaps.
PY: such checks are reported, but only in part, for example the paper says the result held without showing the numbers.
PN: the checks give little comfort, for example one alternative analysis resting on a single guess.
N: the paper reports no such checks. An analysis that puts a value into each gap and then treats the data as complete shows nothing about whether the gaps distort the result.

questions.details:
Answer this question in every case; do not answer NA. When the paper does not say how many results are missing, or why, judge from the outcome and the condition: could being unwell, or getting better, keep someone from being assessed?
Look in: the flow diagram and the text on withdrawals, losses to follow-up and missed visits, for the reasons given. In a time-to-event analysis, a participant who left follow-up early counts as missing.
Y: the reasons given are, or could well be, tied to how participants were doing, for example they stopped coming because they got worse, got better, or had a side effect.
PY: the paper gives no reasons, or reasons for only some participants, and for this outcome how a participant was doing could plausibly decide whether they were assessed, as it can for most clinical outcomes. Reasons left unreported are not a ground for NI.

N: every missing result has a stated reason that cannot be tied to how the participant was doing, for example a blood sample spoiled in the laboratory or a data file lost.

PN: the signs lean the other way.

PN: an effect on this outcome is unlikely, though it cannot be excluded.

NI: the paper does not describe the departures well enough to judge.

questions.details:

study.name: Domain D1: bias arising from the randomisation process (judged once for the trial)

questions.details:
Look in: the methods paragraph on randomisation, any supplement, and a protocol the paper cites.
Y: the paper names a chance mechanism, for example permuted blocks from statistical software or a randomisation website. Minimisation also counts as chance here.
PY: the paper names no mechanism, but what it does say makes a proper one the likely choice, for example the list was drawn up in advance by a statistician with no part in recruitment.
PN: details in the paper hint that the order could be foreseen, without saying so.
N: the group followed something other than chance that someone could know in advance and so predict or steer, for example the room a participant was admitted to.
NI: the paper says the trial was randomised and nothing about how.
questions.headline: Did chance alone decide which group each participant joined?

questions.details:
Look in: the methods, for who kept the allocation list, how the enrolling team learned each group, and whether enrolment came first.
Y: the group was released by a system or person outside the enrolling team, only once the participant was registered, so the team could neither foresee nor swap it.
PY: the paper names a safeguard of this kind but leaves gaps, for example it does not say who prepared the materials or when the group became known.
PN: the method the paper describes left the next assignment within the enrolling team's reach, for example materials kept by that team with no safeguard stated, though nothing shows anyone looked.
N: the enrolling team, or the participants, could see, predict or alter what came next, for example because the list was open to them or the order followed a pattern.
NI: the paper says nothing about how the assignment was kept from the enrolling team.
questions.headline: Was the next assignment out of reach of the people enrolling participants until each participant's enrolment was final?

questions.details:
Look in: the baseline table (characteristics by group) and the flow diagram's count randomised to each group; failing those, any sentence in the paper comparing the groups at the start. Judge from what is reported about the groups, not from the paper's account of how it randomised.
Y: something chance can hardly explain. In the baseline table: a strong predictor of this kind of outcome, or the outcome's own starting value, is unequal enough between groups to sway the result; many more rows differ than chance would give; or nearly every row matches too closely. In the flow diagram: group sizes far from the planned split.
PY: there are signs of this kind, but they are not clear-cut.
PN: nothing stands out, but the evidence is thin: the baseline table is short or leaves out characteristics that matter for this outcome, or the paper gives no numbers by group and only states in its text that the groups were alike at the start.
N: the baseline numbers for the randomised groups show them alike at the start, or differing only as much as random allocation would be expected to make them. One or two rows with a p-value under 0.05 in a long table are what chance alone produces.

Did chance alone decide which group each participant joined?
Look in: the methods paragraph on randomisation, any supplement, and a protocol the paper cites.
Y: the paper names a chance mechanism, for example permuted blocks from statistical software or a randomisation website. Minimisation also counts as chance here.
PY: the paper names no mechanism, but what it does say makes a proper one the likely choice, for example the list was drawn up in advance by a statistician with no part in recruitment.
PN: details in the paper hint that the order could be foreseen, without saying so.
N: the group followed something other than chance that someone could know in advance and so predict or steer, for example the room a participant was admitted to.
NI: the paper says the trial was randomised and nothing about how.

Was the next assignment out of reach of the people enrolling participants until each participant's enrolment was final?
Look in: the methods, for who kept the allocation list, how the enrolling team learned each group, and whether enrolment came first.
Y: the group was released by a system or person outside the enrolling team, only once the participant was registered, so the team could neither foresee nor swap it.
PY: the paper names a safeguard of this kind but leaves gaps, for example it does not say who prepared the materials or when the group became known.
PN: the method the paper describes left the next assignment within the enrolling team's reach, for example materials kept by that team with no safeguard stated, though nothing shows anyone looked.
N: the enrolling team, or the participants, could see, predict or alter what came next, for example because the list was open to them or the order followed a pattern.
NI: the paper says nothing about how the assignment was kept from the enrolling team.

Do the groups, as they stood at the start, look different in a way that hints the randomisation went wrong?

PN: details in the paper hint that the order could be foreseen, without saying so.
N: the group followed something other than chance that someone could know in advance and so predict or steer, for example the room a participant was admitted to.
NI: the paper says the trial was randomised and nothing about how.

Was the next assignment out of reach of the people enrolling participants until each participant's enrolment was final?
Look in: the methods, for who kept the allocation list, how the enrolling team learned each group, and whether enrolment came first.
Y: the group was released by a system or person outside the enrolling team, only once the participant was registered, so the team could neither foresee nor swap it.
PY: the paper names a safeguard of this kind but leaves gaps, for example it does not say who prepared the materials or when the group became known.
PN: the method the paper describes left the next assignment within the enrolling team's reach, for example materials kept by that team with no safeguard stated, though nothing shows anyone looked.
N: the enrolling team, or the participants, could see, predict or alter what came next, for example because the list was open to them or the order followed a pattern.
NI: the paper says nothing about how the assignment was kept from the enrolling team.

Do the groups, as they stood at the start, look different in a way that hints the randomisation went wrong?
Look in: the baseline table (characteristics by group) and the flow diagram's count randomised to each group; failing those, any sentence in the paper comparing the groups at the start. Judge from what is reported about the groups, not from the paper's account of how it randomised.
Y: something chance can hardly explain. In the baseline table: a strong predictor of this kind of outcome, or the outcome's own starting value, is unequal enough between groups to sway the result; many more rows differ than chance would give; or nearly every row matches too closely. In the flow diagram: group sizes far from the planned split.
PY: there are signs of this kind, but they are not clear-cut.
PN: nothing stands out, but the evidence is thin: the baseline table is short or leaves out characteristics that matter for this outcome, or the paper gives no numbers by group and only states in its text that the groups were alike at the start.
N: the baseline numbers for the randomised groups show them alike at the start, or differing only as much as random allocation would be expected to make them. One or two rows with a p-value under 0.05 in a long table are what chance alone produces.
NI: the paper says nothing about what the randomised groups were like at the start: no numbers by group and no statement comparing them. A table of only the participants who stayed to the end is not baseline numbers for the randomised groups.
